newsitem.title: USA: Perot blasts Clinton for refusing to rule out pardons.
newsitem.headline: Perot blasts Clinton for refusing to rule out pardons.

text.p: Reform Party presidential candidate Ross Perot blasted President Bill Clinton on Monday for refusing to rule out granting pardons to figures involved in the Whitewater investigation.
Speaking at a medical conference here, Perot accused Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole of carefully avoiding the real issues during their televised debate on Sunday night.

The Texas billionaire, who was excluded from the debate, condemned Clinton's refusal to rule out granting pardons to people involved in Whitewater, a many-pronged investigation into the Clintons' real estate and financial affairs.

Perot told thousands of doctors attending a conference of the American College of Surgeons that Clinton had "a number of associates who have gone to jail on financial issues that he was allegedly connected to."

"Can you believe that...he (Clinton) will not look the American people in the eye and say: 'If you reelect me as president, I will not use that power to pardon my friends,' because if I don't they're going to talk about me and do a plea bargain?
"Is it asking too much of the president to promise that he won't do that? I hope not," Perot said.

During the debate in Hartford, Connecticut, Clinton refused to rule out pardons, but vowed no one would receive special treatment. "There's been no consideration of it, no discussion of it. I'll tell you this, I will not give anyone special treatment and I will strictly adhere to the law," Clinton said in response to an issue raised by Dole.

One figure involved in the Whitewater investigation, Susan McDougal, is in jail for refusing to answer questions from an independent prosecutor about the president's role. Speculation has centred on whether Clinton would pardon her and others if re-elected.
Perot said Dole and Clinton "carefully avoided the serious problems" during the 90-minute debate. He criticised the decision of the bipartisan Commission on Presidential Debates to exclude him.

Perot said he met "all the objective criteria" for taking part "but five Democrats and five Republicans decided...we want a nice, tight little theatrical event and we don't want the real issues laid out here during the campaign because the American people will remember we said we would do these things and we did not do them."

Perot won 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992. This year, he has garnered only single-digit support in opinion polls and the commission said only Clinton and Dole had a realistic change of being elected president. The courts have rejected Perot's legal challenge to the decision.
Because of his exclusion from the debate, issues such as campaign reform, campaign finance reform and lobbying reform would not be changed, Perot said.

America had a five trillion dollar debt which would grow to seven trillion dollars by the year 2000, he said. "You didn't get that impression based on what they said last night thought, right?" Perot said.

He said the United States had serious financial problems that had to be dealt with now. "If we don't, we're going to have a financial meltdown and millions of people are going to suffer for decades," he said.
Perot also urged doctors to put together their own plan for healthcare in the 21st century.
